malwareList.name: Virus (Vital Information Resources Under Siege)
malwareList.spreadMechanism: Attaches itself to an executable program/file. Requires human action (running infected file) to replicate and spread.
malwareList.damage: Corrupts files, deletes data, alters system settings.
malwareList.historicalFirst: Creeper (1971) on ARPANET; Brain (1986) was first IBM PC virus created by two Pakistani brothers.

malwareList.name: Worm
malwareList.spreadMechanism: Self-replicating standalone program. DOES NOT require a host file or user intervention. Spreads autonomously over computer networks exploiting software vulnerabilities.
malwareList.damage: Consumes massive network bandwidth, crashes servers.
malwareList.historicalFirst: Morris Worm (1988) written by Robert Tappan Morris.

malwareList.name: Trojan Horse
malwareList.spreadMechanism: Disguises itself as legitimate, useful software (e.g., free game, codec, utility). Once installed, secretly executes a malicious payload.
malwareList.keyDifference: CANNOT replicate itself (unlike viruses and worms). Often installs backdoors.

malwareList.name: Ransomware
malwareList.spreadMechanism: Encrypts victim's critical files using unbreakable asymmetric cryptography and demands ransom (usually in Bitcoin/cryptocurrency) for the decryption key.
malwareList.notableExamples: WannaCry (2017, exploited NSA EternalBlue exploit), NotPetya, LockBit.

malwareList.name: Spyware & Keylogger
malwareList.spreadMechanism: Secretly monitors user activities, captures keystrokes (banking passwords, credit card numbers), web history, and sends to attackers.
malwareList.mitigation: Virtual on-screen keyboards used by banks to defeat hardware/software keyloggers.

malwareList.name: Rootkit
malwareList.spreadMechanism: Collection of software tools that grants privileged root/administrator access while actively concealing its presence from OS and antivirus tools by subverting the kernel.

malwareList.name: Botnet & Zombies
malwareList.spreadMechanism: Network of infected internet-connected devices (bots/zombies) controlled remotely by a 'Bot Herder' via Command and Control (C2) servers. Used to launch massive DDoS attacks.

attacks.name: Phishing
attacks.desc: Fraudulent communication (usually email) disguised as trustworthy entity (e.g. Bank SBI, RBI) to trick user into revealing sensitive credentials.

attacks.name: Spear Phishing
attacks.desc: Highly targeted phishing aimed at a specific individual or organization with personalized details.

attacks.name: Whaling
attacks.desc: Phishing targeted specifically at high-profile senior executives (CEOs, CFOs, Board members).

attacks.name: Vishing (Voice Phishing)
attacks.desc: Phone call scams pretending to be bank customer care demanding OTP or CVV.

attacks.name: Smishing (SMS Phishing)
attacks.desc: Fraudulent text messages containing malicious links claiming account deactivation or lottery reward.

attacks.name: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM)
attacks.desc: Attacker secretly intercepts and relays communications between two parties who believe they are communicating directly (mitigated by TLS certificates and HSTS).

attacks.name: DoS & DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service)
attacks.desc: Overwhelming a target server or banking portal with massive floods of bogus traffic to exhaust server resources and deny service to genuine bank customers.

attacks.name: SQL Injection (SQLi)
attacks.desc: Inserting malicious SQL query statements via web application input fields (login box) to manipulate backend database and extract secret records.

attacks.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
attacks.desc: Injecting malicious client-side JavaScript scripts into trusted websites visited by other users to steal session cookies.

attacks.name: Zero-Day Vulnerability
attacks.desc: A security flaw that is unknown to the software vendor and has zero days of patch protection when actively exploited.

ciaTriad.confidentiality: Ensures information is accessible only to authorized entities (achieved via Encryption).
ciaTriad.integrity: Guarantees data is not altered or tampered with in transit (achieved via Cryptographic Hashing).
ciaTriad.availability: Ensures systems and data are readily accessible to authorized users when needed (resilience against DoS).

ciphers.mechanism: Uses the SAME single secret key for both encryption and decryption.
ciphers.algorithms: DES (56-bit, obsolete), 3DES, AES (Advanced Encryption Standard - 128, 192, 256-bit, worldwide standard), Blowfish, RC4.
ciphers.speed: Very fast, computationally lightweight. Key distribution is challenging.

ciphers.mechanism: Uses a KEY PAIR: Public Key (freely shared, used to encrypt) and Private Key (kept strictly secret, used to decrypt).
ciphers.algorithms: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman), ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography), Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, DSA.
ciphers.speed: Slower than symmetric, computationally intensive. Solves key distribution problem.

hashingVsEncryption.encryption: Two-way function. Plaintext can be encrypted into ciphertext and decrypted back into plaintext using the appropriate key.
hashingVsEncryption.hashing: One-way mathematical function (Hash Function). Takes arbitrary input and produces fixed-length digest (e.g. SHA-256 produces 256 bits). Cannot be reversed. Used for password storage and integrity verification.

digitalSignature.definition: Mathematical scheme for demonstrating the authenticity and integrity of digital messages/documents.
digitalSignature.signingProcess: Sender generates hash of message -> encrypts hash using SENDER'S PRIVATE KEY = Digital Signature.
digitalSignature.verificationProcess: Receiver decrypts signature using SENDER'S PUBLIC KEY to recover original hash -> computes new hash of received message -> if both match, signature is authentic!
digitalSignature.properties: Guarantees: 1. Authenticity, 2. Non-Repudiation (sender cannot deny having sent it), 3. Data Integrity.

sections.title: Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 & CERT-In
sections.enacted: Passed in May 2000, notified on October 17, 2000. Major amendment in 2008 (effective October 27, 2009). Based on UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce.

keySections.crime: Penalty and compensation for damage to computer systems (unauthorized copying, introducing virus, denying access).
Tampering with computer source documents (up to 3 years imprisonment or fine up to ₹2 lakh).
Computer-related offences / Hacking (up to 3 years imprisonment or fine up to ₹5 lakh).
Punishment for dishonestly receiving stolen computer resource or communication device.
Punishment for identity theft (using electronic signature, password of another person).
Punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource (phishing scams).
Punishment for violation of privacy (capturing/publishing private images without consent).
Punishment for Cyber Terrorism (attacks on critical infrastructure; punishable with life imprisonment).
Criminalized sending offensive messages through communication services. STRUCK DOWN by Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) as unconstitutional.

certIn.name: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In)
certIn.established: January 2004 under Section 70B of the IT Act.
certIn.role: National nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents, issuing security advisories, handling incident response for Indian cyber space.
